text.p: The following are the main stories from Tuesday morning's Austrian newspapers:
DER STANDARD
- Austrian civil servants, police officials and university teachers have threatened to industrial action if the government failed to act on their grievances over cost-cutting.

- Labour unions of the police and civil servants in the finance ministry and the environment ministry have threatened to take industrial action if the government continues with its planned austerity measures.

- The ministries of justice, interior and foreign affairs will present a 130-page report on the government's involvement in the release in 1989 of Iranians suspected of murdering three Kurdish leaders today. The interior ministry has admitted it made mistakes but also criticised the judiciary.
- The government wants to tighten gun laws after a 15-year-old killed his teacher with his father's hand gun a week ago.
- Die Erste savings bank and GiroCredit will create a common real estate group now that Die Erste holds an 83-percent majority in GiroCredit.
- Raiffeisen bank is reported to have lost interest in taking over the government's 17-percent-stake in postal savings bank PSK.
- In the planned new structure of the Vienna stock exchange both investors and issuers want to hold a 50-percent stake in the public limited company.

- Austria's Finance Minister Rudolf Edlinger said at the EU finance ministers' council in Brussels he opposed the Commission's monetaristic concept of a balanced budget as necessary for membership of the European Economic and Monetary Union.
- Papermaker Steyrermuehl has reported net profits of 134 million schillings in 1996 after losses of 164 million the year before. However the company says it could see a loss this year again too.
- Luxury hosiery maker Wolford expects turnover to rise 11 percent to 1.66 billion schillings in 1996.
DIE PRESSE

- Chancellor Viktor Klima said in a speech that Austria is under no time pressure to become a member of Nato as it is not bound by the same rules as the eastern European countries. But he said a referendum would be necessary in advance.
- Today the elections for Austria's student union starts. More than 220,000 university students are allowed to vote.
- Investor SBC Warburg is searching for the best privatisation mode for postal savings bank PSK.
- The new telecommunications law is not expected to be ready until autumn even though the EU is stepping up pressure for the market to be opened up.
KURIER

- Economics Minister Hannes Farnleitner is pushing for a speedy liberalisation of Austria's electricty market. In 1999 the market should be open to more than 300 major clients. The regional protection of Austria's energy companies is expected to be lifted by 1998.
WIRTSCHAFTSBLATT
- Conservatives are criticising the reform of the insolvency law as they say the restructuring schemes are not practicable.
